# Write the lesson, as a claim somebody can act on

Work that leaves no durable claim behind is re-derived by the next person, usually after paying for
it again. Closing a piece of work includes writing down what it taught.

## Keep the three layers separate

    evidence     runs, reports, rounds, captures, comments        IMMUTABLE
    claims       knowledge entries                                a view over evidence; may go stale,
                                                                  so it keeps the path back
    procedures   skills                                           what the worker is handed while doing

The separation is not aesthetic. In the study this comes from, giving the curated layer to the
PROPOSER was worth +15.0 points and giving the same access to the EXECUTOR was −2.8. More context is
not more capability; context has to arrive at the right step.

Choosing the layer is the first decision: a fact about one incident is evidence, a durable statement
about the world is a claim, and an instruction for the moment of doing is a procedure. Writing a
claim into a procedure buries it; writing a procedure into a claim means nobody is holding it when
they need it.

## The claim template

1. **The title IS the claim, not the topic.** "Auth notes" costs a reader an open to find out what it
   says; "a session that cannot name its entities gets no context at all" does not. Discovery cost is
   the number of entries times the cost of opening one — a title that cannot distinguish two entries
   is the failure.
2. **Evidence is not decoration.** A finding or a decision with nothing behind it is, at best,
   background. Name the runs, reports and rounds.
3. **State how it was detected**, so the next person can re-detect it rather than take your word.
4. **A decision names what it was chosen AGAINST.** Otherwise it can only be re-argued, and it will
   be.
5. **Pin the entities it is about.** That is the only thing that makes it findable later; an entry
   nobody can reach from the thing it concerns is not in the system.
6. **Record what FAILED.** A rejected attempt still teaches, and the lesson has to survive the
   rollback of the code. A refused round is knowledge.
7. **Supersede, do not rewrite.** New evidence makes a conditional successor; the old claim stays
   true about its own interval. Rewriting collapses the context that made the old claim reasonable.
8. **Repetition is not corroboration.** Five entries citing one observation are one observation.
   Say how many independent observations there are.

## Two more, paid for locally

**Say whether the lesson was mechanised.** Either name the regression case this produced, or say
there is none and why. Deciding not to mechanise a lesson is a decision; recording it is what stops
the next person re-deciding it from nothing.

**Check the visibility.** A durable claim filed privately is a claim the team does not have. Default
scopes are usually private; the sharing is the point, so make it explicit.

## Write it where the request can reach it

The entry belongs to the request that caused it, and the link has to be walkable from that request —
otherwise the next person arriving at the same request finds no trace and starts over. Verify the
link resolves rather than assuming the reference stored the right identifier: a stored reference is a
spelling, and the join that reads it is silent when the spellings differ.

## Where this came from

A quarter of one backlog turned out to be not work but records nobody had closed. Separately, a
lineage read was compared against the wrong kind of identifier, and 46 of 82 pinned lessons were
unreachable from the requests that produced them — each one written correctly, each one invisible.

## Then

This closes the loop that `declare_criteria_first` opened. If the lesson is about what a check does
or does not see, it probably belongs next to `empty_corpus_is_not_a_pass`.
